title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: The Fog and the Dust

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, passionate reading of what many consider Charles Dickens's darkest and most dazzling novel.
I'm your host, and over the course of this series we'll be moving through the novel passage by passage — the river, the dust-heaps, the drawing rooms, the disguises, the deaths.
Our Mutual Friend was Dickens's last completed novel, published in 1865, and it is extraordinary — a book about money, identity, and what it means to be found or lost in a city that devours people.
To help us unpack it, I have three exceptional companions.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who is obsessed — in the best possible way — with how great fiction is architecturally built, sentence by sentence.
She makes the machinery of craft feel like a thrilling discovery rather than a technical exercise.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose touchstone is always the moral imagination — the way a novel reveals and tests individual character.
He is beautifully read, occasionally withering, and always illuminating.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic novel audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive — approaches every text as a performer first.
He hears the rhythms, the comic timing, the moments Dickens wrote for the voice rather than the page.
We begin today where the novel itself begins — with atmosphere, with the Thames, and with a body in the water.
What strikes me first about this novel — and it never quite leaves you — is the quality of dread that Dickens manages to sustain.
It isn't the theatrical dread of a ghost story. It's something quieter and stranger — a sense that identity itself is unstable, that the ground beneath your feet might give way.
And nowhere is that more nakedly expressed than in John Harmon's account of the drugged attack — his own dissolution of self.
He writes — and I can't resist reading this aloud —

"I saw a figure like myself lying dressed in my clothes on a bed. What might have been, for anything I knew, a silence of days, weeks, months, years, was broken by a violent wrestling of men all over the room."
That phrase — a silence of days, weeks, months, years — is breathtaking in its compression.
Dickens takes the rupture of conscious time and turns it into a list — and the list itself enacts the terror of not knowing.
What Oliver is identifying there is one of the most sophisticated things Dickens does in this novel — he weaponises syntax.
The sentence about the silence doesn't describe disorientation — it performs it.
And then there's the moment when Harmon sees the double — the figure dressed in his own clothes.
That's not merely gothic atmosphere — that is the novel's central problem made flesh: who is John Harmon, really, if someone else can wear his identity and die in his place?
The plot mechanism and the psychological truth are the same device. That's beautiful architecture.
I take Eleanor's point about the architecture, though I'd frame it slightly differently.
What Dickens is dramatising in that passage is a profound moral emergency — the loss not merely of consciousness but of moral agency.
Harmon cannot act, cannot choose, cannot even name himself. He is, as the passage so bleakly puts it, unable to have said that his name was John Harmon.
And then the same passage reveals that Radfoot's fate was a mirror of the fate intended for Harmon himself.

"Radfoot had been murdered by some unknown hands for the money for which he would have murdered me, and that probably we had both been shot into the river from the same dark place into the same dark tide."
The same dark place, the same dark tide. Dickens does not reach for metaphor there — he simply repeats, and the repetition is more devastating than any flourish could be.
Edmund has put his finger on something that I feel whenever I read this novel aloud — the rhythm of doubling.
Two men, two fates, two bodies in the same black river. And yet they were supposed to be one.
And there's a passage later that plays a completely different register — the train crossing the river — which, for my money, is one of the great set-pieces Dickens ever wrote.
Listen to this — and really listen to the velocity of it:

"the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded in the rush of smoke and steam and glare."
That sentence physically accelerates as you read it. The connectives — 'and... and... and' — they are the pistons firing.
And then it hits the river — and the bomb-shell image arrives with absolute precision.
The polysyndeton — that deliberate piling of 'and' — is doing extraordinary work there.
But what I find even more arresting is what comes immediately after — where Dickens pivots from the train to Father Time himself.
He writes that the train goes "straight to its end, as Father Time goes to his" — and suddenly the mechanical and the eternal are the same thing.
The novel is full of these moments where the mundane and the cosmic briefly occupy the same sentence.
That is Dickens at the very peak of his powers — and it's why this novel, above almost any other, rewards close reading.
The river and the train — ancient and modern, patient and violent — already we can see the novel holding opposites in the same frame.

In our next segment, we'll be looking more closely at the novel's great theme of money — the dust-heaps, the inheritance, and what Dickens understood about wealth's peculiar power to corrupt and to reveal.
Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've spent the last hour tracing the river and the dust-heaps — the great engines of wealth and death in this novel.
Now we turn to what money does to people — how it transforms, corrupts, or occasionally, surprisingly, redeems them.
With us, as ever, are Eleanor Hartley, whose attention to the architecture of Dickens's prose is simply unmatched.
Sir Edmund Leigh, who will keep us honest whenever we mistake social argument for literary art.
And Oliver Trevelyan, who has spent more time inside these characters' voices than almost any living reader.
Eleanor — I want to start with the Boffins, because before we can talk about transformation and money, we need to talk about goodness.
Dickens gives us something almost embarrassingly direct on this subject. What do you make of it?
What Dickens does with the Boffins is formally audacious, actually.
He doesn't trust us to infer their goodness from behaviour alone — he breaks open the narration and states it as law.
There's a passage where the narrator steps forward with the confidence of someone who has thought this through entirely.
"For, Evil often stops short at itself and dies with the doer of it; but Good, never."
That final word — 'never' — sitting alone after the semicolon — is one of the most deliberately placed words in the whole novel.
Dickens has earned it structurally — through Boffin's entire trajectory — but he also just plants it there like a flag.
It's a novelist saying: this is what I believe, and I'm not going to dress it up.
I'm glad you locate it in belief rather than programme, Eleanor.
Because what strikes me is that Dickens is not constructing a sociological thesis here — he is writing moral theology in the tradition of the English sermon.
The Boffins are 'ignorant and unpolished' — Dickens says so plainly — yet they have been guided by 'a religious sense of duty and desire to do right.'
That phrasing is not accidental.
Dickens is making precisely Burke's point — that virtue is not the product of education or refinement but of character, slowly shaped by ordinary life.
The hard master who exploited them 'had never been so warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it.'
Even wickedness, in this moral universe, is compelled to pay homage to goodness.
What I keep coming back to, performing Boffin, is that the goodness is never abstract — it's always embodied.
There's a scene where Boffin recounts seeing the boy John Harmon — seven years old, being packed off to a foreign school, alone.
And you hear Boffin's voice — rough, ungrammatical, entirely without literary pretension — and it absolutely breaks your heart.
Listen to this — the detail of Mrs Boffin kneeling at the fire.
"There was his little scanty travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the steamboat...
Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks;

but seeing the tears come into the child's eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, 'I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!'"
'Pictur of a full-blown rose.' That's Boffin's grammar — not Dickens's — and yet it's the most tender phrase in the chapter.
The inarticulate speaker finds language that the articulate speaker could never quite reach.
And what Dickens does structurally with that memory is almost cruel in its precision.
The boy's look — 'as if it was in pain — in agony' — doesn't fade with time. Mrs Boffin carries it for years, waking at night.
Boffin says it 'gently wore out, as many things do' — and that qualification is devastating.
Because what wore out wasn't the love — it was the sharpness of the grief.
The love, as the narrator has just told us, never stops. Good never dies.
That continuity between the two passages is quite beautiful — Dickens the novelist and Boffin the witness singing the same note in entirely different registers.
But the novel also shows us goodness besieged — and destroyed, in one case, entirely.
I'm thinking of Bradley Headstone — and what becomes of him when obsession takes the place of every other faculty.
Eleanor, you've been sitting with some very dark passages on that front.
Headstone is the novel's most disturbing creation, I think — because he's the dark mirror of Boffin.
Where the Boffins are transformed by love, Headstone is consumed by hatred — and Dickens renders that consumption with horrifying specificity.
There's a passage where Bradley, after the attack on Eugene Wrayburn, mentally replays the murder — correcting it, improving it.
"Supposing his head had been held down under water for a while. Supposing the first blow had been truer. Supposing he had been shot. Supposing he had been strangled.
Suppose this way, that way, the other way. Suppose anything but getting unchained from the one idea, for that was inexorably impossible."
The anaphora of 'Supposing' — six times in rapid succession — mimics the obsessive mind's inability to stop.
The rhythm enacts the pathology. That's what I mean by Dickens constructing his effects at the level of the sentence.
I find Headstone genuinely frightening in a way that purely comic or sentimental Dickens villains are not.
Because his tragedy is Shakespearean in its logic: the very act intended to destroy his rival ensures that rival's happiness.
Dickens states this with magnificent compression in a passage I keep returning to.
"That he had dipped his hands in blood, to mark himself a miserable fool and tool."
'Fool and tool' — the rhyme is almost too neat, and yet it works perfectly because it sounds like fate mocking him.
The directing power — Providence, Fate, whatever one calls it — has overreached him, as Dickens explicitly says.
And Bradley, in 'his impotent mad rage,' can do nothing but bite and tear at himself.
I've performed that passage, and I'll tell you — it's one of the hardest things to voice, precisely because the rhythm does so much of the work.
If you read it at the wrong pace, you lose the trance-like quality — the sense that Bradley is no longer quite choosing to think these thoughts.
And then Dickens gives you what I think of as the death portrait — Bradley sitting through the night, rigid, watching the fire.
"Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard,
its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating."
'The very texture and colour of his hair degenerating.' That's not metaphor — that's Dickens watching a man decompose while still living.
And all the while, Riderhood sits opposite — which is its own kind of horror, because Riderhood is the thing Bradley has become.
That image of the charmed flame is doing extraordinary work.
Fire in this novel is almost always ambiguous — warming Mrs Boffin and the child John Harmon on one side, destroying Headstone on the other.
The same element that Mrs Boffin uses to warm a freezing child — 'kneels down at the fire, warms her two open hands' — is here a force of annihilation.
Dickens doesn't announce that contrast — he trusts us to feel it across hundreds of pages.
That kind of structural patience is what separates the great novels from the merely brilliant ones.
We should touch on the child passage too — c18:p149 — because it connects Lizzie's world to this larger picture of what poverty actually does to the young.
Lizzie Hexam is describing a child — ailing, surrounded from birth by degradation.
Oliver — there's a line there that I think lands like a fist.
It does — and it's the kind of parenthetical that only Dickens can pull off, because it's both grammatical aside and moral indictment simultaneously.
Lizzie says of this poor child — and I want to read this exactly as written.
"This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley."
'If she ever had one.' Five words tucked into a subordinate clause — and they do more damage than a paragraph of outrage could.
The casual doubt about whether this child ever possessed the most basic object of infancy — that's the whole horror of the scene compressed into a conditional clause.
And Lizzie delivers it without self-pity, to her brother — which makes it even quieter, and even more devastating.
What moves me about that moment is that it is Lizzie speaking — who has herself come from the margins of this same world.
She does not sentimentalise the child, nor does she excuse the father — 'a weak wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober.'
Yet she adds, almost immediately, 'But a good workman too, at the work he does' — which is Dickens refusing to allow even the degraded to be entirely without dignity.
That is the moral imagination I spoke of earlier — not programme, but the novelist's instinct that every soul contains its own peculiar complexity.
Good, never — and also: dignity, never quite extinguished.
That feels like the beating heart of what this novel is doing with money and transformation.
Wealth corrupts, want destroys, hatred consumes — but goodness, in Boffin's rough grammar and Lizzie's quiet voice, persists.
After the break, we'll be looking at the river — its dead, its living, and the extraordinary people who work both shores.

segments.title: The Plot Thickens: John Harmon's Secret

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've reached one of the novel's great structural mysteries: the secret identity of John Harmon.
A man presumed drowned, a fortune left unclaimed, and a stranger who appears in the Boffins' household under a false name.
To unpack this, we have Dr Eleanor Hartley, who will be watching how Dickens engineers our readerly suspicion at the level of the sentence.
Sir Edmund Leigh, who suspects the real interest lies not in the plot mechanism but in the moral weight it places on individual character.
And Oliver Trevelyan, who has performed more Dickens than most people have read, and who finds in these chapters a kind of theatrical genius.
Let's begin with the Boffins — because before we can understand what John Harmon's secret costs him, we need to understand what the Boffins did for him.
Mr Boffin's testimony about old Harmon's cruelty is one of the great comic-tragic set pieces in the novel.
It's funny and appalling in equal measure — and Dickens keeps both registers perfectly balanced.
Listen to how Boffin tells Lightwood about old Harmon's rages.

'I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet — she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head — and send it spinning across the yard.'
The parenthetical about the bonnet — that's the thing.
Dickens gives us the exact hat — a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience — in the middle of a scene of genuine violence.
And then the curtain line: 'Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.'
Two words. Repeated. You cannot top that for dramatic economy.
Oliver's right that the repetition is devastating — but I want to notice why it works structurally.
Boffin is narrating this to a lawyer, in what is ostensibly a legal and financial conversation.
And yet the emotional weight keeps breaking through — the love for young John, the remembered violence, the grief.
That gap between the formal occasion and the feeling pouring out of it is where Dickens does his best work.
And this passage sets up something Mrs Boffin says just a chapter later that I find genuinely haunting.
She proposes adopting an orphan child and naming him John Harmon — the dead boy's name.
'Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him.'
She wants to keep the name alive — to redirect the money toward a living child who can actually use it.
The irony, of course, is that John Harmon is not dead — and is about to walk into their house.
Eleanor has identified the irony precisely, and it is a rich one.
But I want to resist the temptation to admire the mechanism at the expense of the moral substance.
Mrs Boffin's impulse is not a plot device — it is an act of goodness.
She has come into money she did not seek, and her first instinct is to use it to honour a dead child and help a living one.
That is not irony — that is character.
The entire machinery of John Harmon's disguise depends on this bedrock of Boffin goodness for its emotional force.
Without understanding what the Boffins suffered for the boy, and what they are willing to do for his memory, the secret identity plot is merely a puzzle.
Edmund is right, and I would add only that Dickens himself was rather pleased with his own puzzle — and said so.
There's an extraordinary moment, almost a note tucked inside the novel, where he addresses the reader directly on this very question.

'I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.'
He is essentially saying: I was not hiding the secret — I was waving a flag at it.
And then — my favourite part — he asks readers to concede the artist 'a little patience.'
It has the exact tone of a man who has been thoroughly misread and is being very gracious about it.
What Dickens is defending there is something genuinely important about how the novel works as an artistic object.
The identity plot isn't a whodunit — it's a structure for exploring what it means to return to a world that has moved on without you.
Harmon watches the Boffins from inside his disguise — watches them grieve for him, watches Mrs Boffin want to adopt an orphan in his name.
That sustained observation is what gives the revelation its moral weight when it finally comes.
I find myself drawn, in this context, to a very different scene — the rooftop where Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren read together.
It stands apart from the identity plot entirely, and yet it illuminates the novel's deepest concern: what can the powerless do with what little they have?
Dickens describes the scene with a peculiar pastoral tenderness.
'Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren. For whom, perhaps with some old instinct of his race, the gentle Jew had spread a carpet... they both pored over one book; both with attentive faces.'
Above the city's squalor, two young women — one crippled, one unlettered — are making themselves a garden of the mind.
The encompassing chimneys, Dickens tells us, look on 'in a state of airy surprise' — as well they might.
There is more hope in that rooftop than in all the Harmon gold.
That image of the rooftop garden is one I return to every time I read this novel.
But there is another scene that seems to me the emotional twin of it — equally quiet, equally charged with mortality.
Eugene Wrayburn's deathbed marriage to Lizzie — the ceremony read over a man who cannot move his hand.
Eleanor has been assigned the passage — I'll let her read it — but I find it almost unbearable in the best possible way.
Oliver's generosity is noted and welcome — because this passage is extraordinary.
Dickens begins by framing the wedding service against death — 'so rarely associated with the shadow of death; so inseparable in the mind from a flush of life and gaiety and hope and health and joy.'
Every word of that is doing double work — it describes the ceremony's usual register and inverts it simultaneously.
And then the gesture that closes the scene — which I find almost impossible to read without stopping.
'When the two plighted their troth, she laid her hand on his and kept it there.'
'When the ceremony was done, and all the rest departed from the room, she drew her arm under his head, and laid her own head down upon the pillow by his side.'
No speech. No declaration. Just the body's quiet act of fidelity.
Dickens does more in two sentences there than most novelists manage in a chapter.
It is, as Eleanor says, a scene of pure moral action expressed through physical gesture.
Lizzie Hexam lays her head beside a dying man she loves and whom society has told her she cannot have.
She does not argue. She does not claim. She simply stays.
That is the novel's answer to all its plots and disguises and mysteries.
Not revelation — but constancy.
Constancy against all that the river and the dust-heaps and the money can do to a person.
We've moved from a spinning bonnet and a dropped woman to a deathbed marriage — and Dickens has made every step of that journey feel inevitable.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the novel's great dark comedy — the world of Veneering and Podsnap, where identity is not hidden but performed, brazenly, in plain sight.

segments.title: Dust and Corruption: The Social Underbelly

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — as seriously as it deserves.
I'm joined today by three remarkable readers, and we're diving into one of the novel's great comic obsessions: dust, money, and the extraordinary ecosystem of greed that surrounds the Boffin fortune.
Eleanor Hartley is here — novelist, critic, and the person I most want beside me when a sentence is doing something technically astonishing.
Sir Edmund Leigh joins us — Oxford don, moralist, and a man who believes that if a novel isn't about character, it isn't about anything.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, audiobook narrator extraordinaire, who hears what the rest of us merely read.
Our focus today is on the great satirical set-pieces around the Boffin household — charity, begging, class performance, and what Dickens does with the sheer comedy of new money meeting old appetite.
Oliver, you've read this novel aloud more times than most people have read it silently — where do you want to begin?
I want to begin with the letters — the avalanche of charity solicitations that buries the Secretary the moment Boffin's name is made public.
Because Dickens does something absolutely wicked here — he gives us the itemised absurdity first.
Fifty-seven churches, forty-two parsonage houses, seven-and-twenty organs — the accumulation is comic but it's also damning.
And then he gives us the crown jewel — the Duke of Linseed's letter.
'Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.'
Six words, and the man is demolished.
'Fat.' 'Double.' That letter doesn't just arrive — it imposes itself.
And when you read the duke's actual letter, it's all flattery and condescension — right up until the postscript, where the three-guinea fee slips in like a pickpocket.
What I love is the parenthetical precision of 'and thoughtful in the postscript' — Dickens places that aside so perfectly.
The narrator pretends to be charmed by the duke, even grateful, and the irony is so controlled it could cut glass.
But what Dickens is really doing structurally is showing us the Secretary's experience — this is filtered through a consciousness of accumulating horror.
The Secretary opens letter after letter, and we open them with him — the form of the passage enacts the experience.
Dickens asks, rhetorically: 'Oh the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold dust of the Golden Dustman!'
That line connects the whole charity circus back to the novel's central metaphor.
Dust as obscuring matter, as rubbish disguised as value — these letters are dust thrown in the eyes.
I'd rather resist the temptation to make this purely a metaphysical reading about the novel's dusty imagery.
What strikes me is rather simpler and rather more devastating: Dickens is writing about the corruption of charity itself.
The duke's letter is not merely comic — it is an indictment of a social system in which benevolence has become transaction.
The man of God who asks for a steward's fee of three guineas has, in Burke's phrase, abandoned the moral imagination entirely.
And the novel knows this — which is precisely why John Harmon, at the close, insists on the unimpeachable goodness of Mr and Mrs Boffin against all this corruption.
We are told, without irony, that he owes everything to their disinterestedness.
'I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness — there are no words to satisfy me — of Mr and Mrs Boffin.'
That is what the novel sets against the Duke of Linseed and his three guineas.
Edmund is absolutely right that the novel earns that moment — but let's not skip the individual beggars, because they are extraordinary.
The corporate beggars with their letters were one thing — but the private correspondence is a whole taxonomy of human desperation and ingenuity.
The line about their documents is the one I never tire of performing.
'They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf.'
Minced veal to a calf — the ratio of the real thing to its sad remnant, stated with absolute comic economy.
And then he gives you the daughters of general officers, 'long accustomed to every luxury of life, except spelling' — and there it is, the knife.
The beggars on horseback, the inspired beggars waiting for the angel's whisper — Dickens is not being cruel; he's being devastatingly precise about how misery performs itself.
The 'beggars of punctual business-habits' are the ones that haunt me — they will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday.
There's a grotesque comedy in that specificity, but there's also genuine darkness underneath.
Dickens is cataloguing types, but the catalogue form is itself a kind of comedy that holds tragedy at arm's length — and then lets it in anyway.
I think this is why the Sloppy passage is so important — Dickens can pivot from savage satire to pure tenderness in a single chapter.
The description of his new suit of mourning clothes is one of the great comic passages in the novel.
The tailor has been instructed to conceal the buttons — and the body simply refuses to cooperate.
'He now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators.'
The body exceeds the class aspiration — and Dickens loves Sloppy for it.
The Argus simile is a stroke of genuine classical wit — quite unexpected in a comic scene about an ungainly young man in ill-fitting clothes.
But what the passage achieves, beneath the comedy, is something rather noble — it shows Mrs Boffin's instinctive generosity of spirit.
She has clothed this extraordinary creature in black as an act of consideration — the joke is on the tailor's art, not on Sloppy's dignity.
And that is what separates the Boffins from the Duke of Linseed — charity as genuine feeling versus charity as social mechanism.
Edmund, I entirely agree — and the hatband is the detail that undoes me every time I read it aloud.
Fluted from crown to brim, terminating in a black bunch 'from which the imagination shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted.'
Imagination shrunk — reason revolted — two entirely different faculties, both defeated by a hat.
There's a music-hall quality to that, but the sentence construction is impeccable — it only works because Dickens has the rhythm exactly right.
Let's bring Silas Wegg into the picture — because Wegg represents something quite different from the charity-seekers: a corruption that is intimate, domestic, and treacherous.
Eleanor, there's a will at the centre of Wegg's scheming — what does that document reveal?
Wegg reads the will aloud to Mr Venus in a scene that is both comic and genuinely sinister — the way a man savours another man's ruin.
The document itself, as Wegg summarises it, has a wonderful bitter clarity.

'Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown.'
The elder Harmon writes his will as a man settling scores with the world — 'quite enough for him' is almost contemptuous even of the bequest.
And Boffin's response to all of this — his entire conduct throughout the novel — is to be precisely the opposite kind of man from old Harmon.
The elder Harmon is Dickens's study in what riches do to a soul that was never generous to begin with.
The will is not an eccentricity — it is a character portrait distilled into legal language.
'Never made friends' — 'ever had a rebellious family' — one hears in those phrases a lifetime of refusal.
And the novel is careful to show that his son John Harmon might have become the same kind of man — had he not been rescued by the Boffins' example.
There's something rather magnificent about Wegg reading that will, though — because he thinks he's found the lever to destroy Boffin.
And he's entirely wrong about the nature of the man he's dealing with — the irony is delicious.
When Harmon finally confronts Wegg and tells him the truth about the fortune, it's one of the great reversals in the novel.
The rage in that speech is real — 'the wonder is that I didn't try to twist your head off, and fling that out of window.'
Dickens gives Harmon genuine physical anger — and earns it, because the audience knows by then what the Boffins have actually done.
And yet there is, amid all this dust and corruption, a passage of pure unhurried happiness — Bella and John Rokesmith's supper.
Eleanor, you've written about what it means when Dickens allows a scene to be simply, quietly delightful — what do you make of this moment?
It's structurally very deliberate — Dickens places this small feast in the office of Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles, surrounded by ledgers and commerce.
And Bella herself names it — she reaches for a fairy tale.

'It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, Somebody's been drinking my milk!'
The fairy tale is invoked — and then the threat is gently removed.
No thunderous growlings, no alarming discoveries — just the meal, and the company, and the joy.
And then that wonderful detail: the two brass knobs of the iron safe staring from a corner 'like the eyes of some dull dragon' — even here, the world watches.
But the dragon is dull — it cannot spoil this.
What strikes me is that Bella's happiness is only possible because she has chosen correctly — chosen the man over the fortune.
This is Dickens's great moral argument — and it is not a social argument, whatever the critics say.
It is a novel about what a human being does with the temptations placed before them — and Bella, in that supper room, has already made her choice.
The dragon in the corner is inert because the people in the room are not enslaved to what it represents.
I've read that passage aloud in recording studios three times now, and I confess I slow down on 'delicious' — it's such a simple word to carry such weight.
'It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made.'
'Or even R. Wilfer' — that 'even' is doing tremendous work.
It extends the circle of happiness outward — father included, joy shared, nothing hoarded.
After all those letters and charity frauds and wills written out of spite — Dickens earns this meal.
Dust and corruption on one side; a delicious repast on the other — and the novel holds both without flinching.
Thank you to Eleanor, Edmund, and Oliver — and to our listeners for staying with us through this extraordinary world Dickens built.
We'll be back in the next segment — going deeper into how the novel handles identity, disguise, and what it means to be known.

segments.title: Laughter in the Shadows: Dickens's Comic Mastery

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart, passage by passage, to see what makes it tick.
I'm your host, and today we're exploring one of the novel's most extraordinary qualities: the way Dickens holds comedy and menace in the same hand.
Our segment is called Laughter in the Shadows, and it couldn't be better named.
With me today are three remarkable readers of this novel.

Dr Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who has spent her career studying how great prose is actually built — the architecture behind the effects we feel but can't always explain.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who reads novels as moral dramas — stories about individual character tested to its limits — and who brings to every discussion a formidable memory and a perfectly calibrated wit.

And Oliver Trevelyan has narrated more classic novels than any living person, and he approaches Dickens the way a great actor approaches Shakespeare — listening first for the rhythm, then for the meaning.
Oliver, I want to start with you, because you've been given a remarkable spread of passages today — from Lady Tippins's electioneering performance to Bradley Headstone lurking on a dark staircase.
What does it feel like, as a performer, to move between those two registers in the same novel?
It feels, honestly, like being handed two entirely different instruments and told to play them both in the same concert.
And the staggering thing about Dickens is that he doesn't apologise for the contrast — he exploits it.
Take Lady Tippins first, because she is one of his supreme comic inventions.
What he does in that passage is give her an entire electioneering speech rendered as gossip — and the gossip is the point.
She rattles on, and the rattling itself is the satire.
Listen to the line where she drops all pretence entirely.
"And we are carrying on this little farce to keep up appearances, and isn't it refreshing!"
The word 'farce' is her word — she names the whole social performance herself, with complete self-satisfaction.
That exclamation mark after 'refreshing' — that's the whole character in a single punctuation mark.
And what's extraordinary is how he sustains the voice for the entire passage without a single authorial interruption.
Dickens just opens the tap and lets Lady Tippins flow.
The structure is brilliant — she begins with mock-ignorance, 'you'll never guess,' and then strings together a series of escalating revelations, each more absurd than the last.
And the sentence where she forgets the baby — that small, perfectly placed parenthesis — tells you everything about how these people value human beings.
The baby is the third dearest friend she has in the world, added as an afterthought.
It's comic, but it's also a little chilling once you see it.
Quite so — though I would add that what makes Lady Tippins remarkable is not merely her cynicism but her transparency.
She does not deceive herself for a single moment.
The Veneerings, by contrast, are among the most thoroughly self-deceived creatures in English fiction — and she uses them as props for her own entertainment.
She says, with magnificent frankness, that they 'know nobody' and that nobody knows them.
"Nobody knows who these Veneerings are, and that they know nobody, and that they have a house out of the Tales of the Genii, and give dinners out of the Arabian Nights."
The Oriental references are not mere decoration — they signal that the Veneerings belong to the world of fantasy, not of honest English life.
It is, if you will, Dickens's way of saying: these people are not real — they are a story someone is telling.
And then Dickens pivots — and I mean pivots completely — to a staircase at night.
The Bradley Headstone passage is one of the most unsettling things in the whole novel, and it's barely a paragraph.
When I read it aloud in the studio, I always pause before that phrase 'the haggard head.'
Because he doesn't say 'Bradley' or 'the man' — he gives us a disembodied, floating head.
The sentence that closes the passage is the one that really haunts me.

"If Lightwood could have seen the face which kept him awake, staring and listening in the darkness outside the door as he spoke of it, he might have been less disposed to sleep, through the remainder of the night."
The conditional — 'if he could have seen' — means Lightwood never does see.
The reader knows, and the character does not — and that is where the dread lives.
The craft there is in the point of view — the omniscient narrator who knows what Lightwood cannot see.
Dickens uses omniscience very selectively — he withholds it throughout most of the novel's plotting — and then deploys it here, in one sentence, to devastating effect.
The structure is almost architectural: a whole paragraph of atmospheric detail building a threshold — the door, the candlelight, the voices — and then the light goes out.
And in the silence and dark, the narrator turns to us and says: here is the thing you are not being shown.
It's an extraordinary move.
One notices that the comedy and the gothic share a common grammar in this novel.
Both Lady Tippins and Bradley Headstone are performing — she for an audience she is cultivating, he for one that cannot see him.
The novel is full of watchers and performers, and Dickens shifts the register from farce to horror simply by changing who is watching whom.
That's a fascinating structural observation, and it brings us to two more comic passages Oliver has been sitting on — both of them, I suspect, giving him enormous pleasure.
Mrs Sprodgkin, the catastrophically weepy parishioner, and then the glorious final disposal of Mr Silas Wegg.
Oliver — shall we start with Mrs Sprodgkin?
Mrs Sprodgkin is a gift — a pure, unalloyed gift from Dickens to anyone who has ever been cornered by a tiresome parishioner at an inopportune hour.
The technical achievement here is how he makes her simultaneously absurd and exhausting — you laugh, but you also feel the weight of her.
The line that gets me every time is this one about her conduct in church.

"She was a member of the Reverend Frank's congregation, and made a point of distinguishing herself in that body, by conspicuously weeping at everything, however cheering, said by the Reverend Frank in his public ministration."
'However cheering' — that qualifier is the entire joke.
She doesn't weep at sad things — that would be respectable — she weeps at everything, indiscriminately, as a performance of piety.

And then there's the detail that she delivers the responsive parts of the service as if lodging a formal complaint with a magistrate — at which point I always break into an involuntary grin in the recording booth.
The phrase 'an infection of absurdity' is the structural key to the whole portrait.
Dickens doesn't just describe her as absurd — he says the absurdity is contagious, that it communicates itself to 'everything with which, and everybody with whom, she came in contact.'
That's a very precise satirical mechanism — she infects situations, not just people.
And then Dickens quietly places the Milveys against her — their 'exemplary sweetness and good-humour' — which is his way of acknowledging real virtue without sentimentalising it.
The comedy doesn't diminish their goodness — it actually illuminates it by contrast.
One should observe that Dickens treats the Milveys with uncommon respect for his own comic purposes.
The Reverend Frank goes out to Mrs Sprodgkin at dawn, 'perfectly knowing that nothing but a cold would come of it.'
That parenthetical resignation is, I would argue, one of the most quietly moving lines in the novel's comic register.
He knows the visit is futile — and goes anyway.
That is a sketch of genuine goodness, rendered without a syllable of preaching — which is rather harder to achieve than satire.
And now, Wegg.
I have been saving Wegg's ejection for last because it is, without question, the most purely satisfying comic disposal in all of English fiction.
The setup is already magnificent — Sloppy, who has been an amiable background presence for most of the novel, suddenly picks Wegg up 'like the sack of flour or coals before mentioned.'
But the punchline — the scavenger's cart — that is something else entirely.
Dickens writes it with the deadpan precision of a stage direction.

"Mr Sloppy's instructions had been to deposit his burden in the road; but, a scavenger's cart happening to stand unattended at the corner, with its little ladder planted against the wheel, Mr S. found it impossible to resist the temptation of shooting Mr Silas Wegg into the cart's contents."
And then — 'A somewhat difficult feat, achieved with great dexterity, and with a prodigious splash.'
'A prodigious splash' — I defy anyone to read that with a straight face.
Wegg ends where he began — in the dust — and Dickens makes it literal.
What I love about that passage is the way Dickens distributes the agency so carefully.
It's not John Harmon who throws Wegg out — it's Sloppy, acting on his own inspired initiative once he sees the cart.
And the narrator steps in as a kind of appreciative critic — 'a somewhat difficult feat, achieved with great dexterity' — as if reviewing a gymnastics display.
The prose style enacts the comedy — the rhythm of that sentence is the rhythm of a triumphant flourish.
And one should not overlook the brief exchange that precedes Wegg's ejection, where the Secretary warns him about insolence.
It is very short — a single sentence — and entirely cold.
"Be careful what insolent liberties you take in that gentleman's presence, or I will throw you after it."
The pronoun 'it' is magnificent — Wegg is already an object in that sentence, before Sloppy has laid a hand on him.
Dickens signals Wegg's moral reduction through grammar, before he signals it through action.
That is not farce — that is something more purposeful and considerably darker.
That feels like exactly the right note to end on — comedy that knows where the darkness is, and uses it.
From Lady Tippins's green fan to Wegg's prodigious splash, this has been a reminder of why Our Mutual Friend rewards such close attention.
Thank you to Eleanor Hartley, Edmund Leigh, and Oliver Trevelyan — and we'll be back shortly with our next segment.

segments.title: The Moral Architecture: Themes and Transformation

utterances.text: Welcome to this segment of Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, where we turn to what I'd call the moral architecture of the novel.
Dickens isn't simply telling a story about money and the Thames — he's constructing an elaborate moral argument about what wealth does to the people it touches.
To explore that, we have three brilliant companions.
Dr Eleanor Hartley, whose eye for narrative craft will help us see how Dickens builds his effects from the sentence up.
Sir Edmund Leigh, who will keep us honest about what this novel is ultimately about — individual character tested by circumstance.
And Oliver Trevelyan, who has read more Dickens aloud than almost anyone living, and hears what the rest of us miss on the page.
Let's begin with John Harmon's extraordinary interior confession — the moment when the architecture of his deception is laid fully bare.
What strikes me first about these chapters is the structural audacity of placing John Harmon's confession so late in the novel.
Dickens has withheld Harmon's interiority for hundreds of pages, and now suddenly we're inside a mind that is extraordinarily scrupulous about its own motives.
The passage where he returns to England is almost a legal cross-examination of the self.
Listen to how Dickens builds that relentless repetition:
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
That triple-hammered anaphora — 'shrinking,' 'shrinking,' 'mistrustful' — it isn't rhetoric for its own sake.
It enacts the psychological condition it describes — a man whose every instinct recoils from his inheritance.
And then there's that extraordinary self-interrogation at the end: 'Now, stop, and so far think it out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.'
Eleanor's absolutely right about that self-interrogation — as a performer it's one of the most technically demanding passages in the whole novel to read aloud.
You have a character who is simultaneously the narrator of his own story and a hostile witness at his own trial.
But what moves me most is the passage where he explains why the whole thing spun so far beyond his original intention.
Dickens gives us this extraordinary sentence about how a man falls into a condition without perceiving what's happening to him.

'When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless.'
That parenthetical — 'never yet for good within his knowledge then' — is devastating in its quiet precision.
The wealth of Harmon's father has never, in John's entire experience of it, done a single good thing.
That little phrase carries the whole weight of the novel's argument.
I want to resist the temptation to read all of this purely as social argument about wealth, compelling as those readings are.
What Dickens is really exploring, I would argue, is the nature of moral timidity — a phrase he himself uses.
Harmon is not simply victimised by his inheritance. He is a man whose capacity for trust has been corroded from childhood.
The passage about proving Bella is quietly extraordinary in that regard.
'The thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
He doesn't say he wishes to test Bella's worth. He says he wishes to prove it — the word implies both an experiment and a hope.
And the phrase 'moral timidity that dates from my childhood' — this is Dickens being rather more psychologically exact than he is usually given credit for.
The man is not wicked. He is damaged. The novel is about whether damaged people can be redeemed — and that, to my mind, is a far richer subject than the iniquities of inherited wealth.
Edmund, I don't think those two readings are in conflict — Dickens is too generous a novelist to let us choose between them.
But I do want to press on the dilemma Dickens constructs for Harmon in chapter thirty-one, because architecturally it's a masterpiece.
Was it for him to have the shame of buying Bella, or the meanness of punishing her?
Coming to life and accepting the inheritance — he buys her. Coming to life and refusing it — he punishes her for her earlier mercenary candour.
It's a logical trap — and the only escape is the one the novel constructs: that Bella must first transform of her own free will, before the trap can be sprung open.
The entire plot mechanism is a moral argument rendered in dramatic form.
And while all this psychological machinery is whirring away, Dickens makes absolutely sure we don't lose the comedy.
Because Mr Boffin is simultaneously the instrument of Bella's testing and a magnificent satirical creation in his own right.
His rant about charity patrons is one of the great comic speeches in the novel — and I defy anyone to read it without grinning.

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
That list just keeps going — it accumulates absurdity the way the Thames accumulates rubbish.
'If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain't he a Patron?' — Boffin has cut straight through the pretension of Victorian philanthropy with one question.
Dickens believed great comedy was the sharpest instrument of moral criticism — and Boffin proves it.
Oliver touches on something I find genuinely fascinating — Boffin as a moral instrument.
But there's another moment of moral reckoning I wish to draw attention to, which is rather less decorous than Boffin's comic philanthropy.
The scene where Harmon finally confronts Silas Wegg — the physical reckoning — is, I think, deeply satisfying precisely because it is visceral.
Dickens gives us the moment with tremendous economy.
'He found himself gripped by the cravat; shaken until his teeth chattered; shoved back, staggering, into a corner of the room; and pinned there.'
Four verbs. Each one a stage of humiliation. Dickens is writing with the precision of a boxing commentator.
There is a puritanical satisfaction in it that Dickens — whatever his sentimental reputation — never entirely suppresses.
The wicked are, in the end, gripped by the cravat. One hopes.
And on that note of perfectly calibrated retribution, we'll take a brief pause before turning to the world of the river — and what it carries beneath the surface.
The moral architecture of Our Mutual Friend, as our guests have shown, is built from damaged psychology, comic outrage, and moments of genuine physical reckoning — sometimes all at once.
Stay with us.
We've ranged across the full width of this extraordinary novel today — from the Thames mud to the drawing rooms, from the schoolroom to the heart.
Before we close, I want to give each of our guests a chance to draw the threads together — to say what, finally, they believe this novel is about at its deepest level.
Oliver, you've spent more hours inside Dickens's sentences than almost anyone alive. Where does Our Mutual Friend leave you?
It leaves me — every single time — with the feeling that I've survived something.
Not endured — survived. There's a violence to this book that never quite lets you go.
And I think it begins — genuinely begins — in the schoolroom. In that extraordinary passage about Charley Hexam's school.
Dickens describes what should be a place of hope and improvement, and makes it one of the most grotesque comic nightmares in English fiction.
He writes — and I have to read this, because the rhythm of it is the whole point —
"An exceedingly and confoundingly perplexing jumble of a school, in fact, where black spirits and grey, red spirits and white, jumbled jumbled jumbled jumbled, jumbled every night."
That repetition isn't madness on his part — it's complete precision. You feel the jumble. You are inside it.
And then the Sunday school executioner — the volunteer boy smoothing the faces of sleeping infants — that image is simultaneously farcical and deeply, deeply cruel.
The novel knows that cruelty and comedy live in the same house. That's what makes it almost unbearable to perform — and completely impossible to put down.
Oliver puts his finger on something essential — that the cruelty and the comedy are structurally inseparable in this book.
But what strikes me, closing the novel, is the way Dickens balances that darkness against moments of almost unbearable tenderness.
Take the scene where old Wilfer blesses Bella's engagement to Rokesmith — the man she has chosen over wealth.
It could so easily be sentimental. Dickens keeps it honest by giving Wilfer this extraordinary, self-delighting speech that is ridiculous and moving at exactly the same time.
He calls Bella — repeatedly, with great relish — 'this mercenary young person distantly related to myself.'
"I admire this mercenary young person distantly related to myself, more in this dress than if she had come to me in China silks, Cashmere shawls, and Golconda diamonds."
That absurd, loving formality — 'distantly related to myself' — is doing everything. It is how a man who can't quite say 'my daughter' says 'my daughter.'
And then he speaks of 'the poverty she has accepted for your sake and the honest truth's' — and it lands like a benediction. It earns every bit of sentiment it spends.
That is the craft I find most astonishing in this novel: the absolute control over when to make you laugh and when to devastate you — and when to do both at once.
Eleanor is quite right, and I want to hold that word — 'benediction' — for a moment.
Because I think what this novel is, at its marrow, is a meditation on moral transformation. On whether a human soul can change — and at what cost.
Bella changes. Wrayburn changes, decisively and painfully. Even Boffin enacts a kind of performance of change to liberate someone else.
But Bradley Headstone cannot change. And the novel's portrait of that impossibility is among the most searching things Dickens ever wrote.
There is a sentence in the Bradley passages that I find — and I don't use the word lightly — philosophically devastating.
"There are fifty doors by which discovery may enter. With infinite pains and cunning, he double locks and bars forty-nine of them, and cannot see the fiftieth standing wide open."
That is not merely a description of a guilty man's psychology. That is a description of every form of willed blindness — in life, in politics, in the soul.
One thinks of Burke on the nature of self-deception: that the mind most desperately engaged in concealment is the last to see what it is hiding.
That is why I resist purely sociological readings of this novel. The deepest wound is always interior.
Edmund, I agree with you completely — and I'd add that the passage just before that sentence makes it even more chilling.
Dickens describes Riderhood tracking Bradley, and writes —
"He was a better follower than Bradley. It had been the calling of his life to slink and skulk and dog and waylay, and he knew his calling well."
'Slink and skulk and dog and waylay' — four verbs, each one nastier than the last. The sentence itself is a pursuit.
And 'he knew his calling well' — that final clause lands with such terrible irony. Here is a man whose vocation is destruction, and he is excellent at it.
Bradley is doomed not because society failed him — though it did — but because he is being hunted by something as relentless and amoral as his own guilt.
The novel earns its ending — violently, grimly, completely.
What I keep returning to is that all of these strands — the grotesque schoolroom, Bella's moral awakening, Bradley's destruction — are held in the same novel.
And not just by plot machinery, but by a single, governing imagination that refuses to sentimentalise or to despair.
The novel ends — as it began — with water. With the Thames. With things that are lost coming back changed.
That is the mutual bond of the title: the bond between all the people the river claims and returns, damages and restores, drowns and resurrects.
I shall simply say this: I have read this novel many times, and it has never once given me the same book twice.
That is, I think, the surest mark of a masterwork. It grows with you. Or perhaps — one simply grows more capable of receiving it.
And on that note, I think we should leave our listeners to receive it — or receive it again — for themselves.
My warmest thanks to Dr. Eleanor Hartley, Sir Edmund Leigh, and Oliver Trevelyan — three readers who have made this novel feel, if anything, larger than when we began.
Our Mutual Friend Unpacked. Thank you for listening.

‘I examined the newspapers every day for tidings that I was missing, but
      saw none. Going out that night to walk (for I kept retired while it was
      light), I found a crowd assembled round a placard posted at Whitehall. It
      described myself, John Harmon, as found dead and mutilated in the river
      under circumstances of strong suspicion, described my dress, described the
      papers in my pockets, and stated where I was lying for recognition. In a
      wild incautious way I hurried there, and there—with the horror of
      the death I had escaped, before my eyes in its most appalling shape, added
      to the inconceivable horror tormenting me at that time when the poisonous
      stuff was strongest on me—I perceived that Radfoot had been murdered
      by some unknown hands for the money for which he would have murdered me,
      and that probably we had both been shot into the river from the same dark
      place into the same dark tide, when the stream ran deep and strong.

Then, the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides
      of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and
      under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over
      the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded
      in the rush of smoke and steam and glare. A little more, and again it
      roared across the river, a great rocket: spurning the watery turnings and
      doublings with ineffable contempt, and going straight to its end, as

c9:p29.text:
These two ignorant and unpolished people had guided themselves so far on
      in their journey of life, by a religious sense of duty and desire to do
      right. Ten thousand weaknesses and absurdities might have been detected in
      the breasts of both; ten thousand vanities additional, possibly, in the
      breast of the woman. But the hard wrathful and sordid nature that had
      wrung as much work out of them as could be got in their best days, for as
      little money as could be paid to hurry on their worst, had never been so
      warped but that it knew their moral straightness and respected it. In its
      own despite, in a constant conflict with itself and them, it had done so.
      And this is the eternal law. For, Evil often stops short at itself and
      dies with the doer of it; but Good, never.
c9:p29.summary: Dickens reflects that the Boffins, though ignorant and unpolished, have been guided by genuine religious duty and moral righteousness that even hardened souls cannot entirely resist.

‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’
c8:p43.summary: Boffin recounts the last time he and Mrs Boffin saw young John Harmon, a seven-year-old being sent to a foreign school, including the poignant moment when Mrs Boffin wept while warming the boy by the fire and embraced him protectively, expressing a desire to save him—a memory that haunted her for years.

Bradley toiled on, chained heavily to the idea of his hatred and his
      vengeance, and thinking how he might have satiated both in many better
      ways than the way he had taken. The instrument might have been better, the
      spot and the hour might have been better chosen. To batter a man down from
      behind in the dark, on the brink of a river, was well enough, but he ought
      to have been instantly disabled, whereas he had turned and seized his
      assailant; and so, to end it before chance-help came, and to be rid of
      him, he had been hurriedly thrown backward into the river before the life
      was fully beaten out of him. Now if it could be done again, it must not be
      so done. Supposing his head had been held down under water for a while.

c67:p57.text:
When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.

Then, they all stood around the bed, and Mr Milvey, opening his book,
      began the service; so rarely associated with the shadow of death; so
      inseparable in the mind from a flush of life and gaiety and hope and
      health and joy. Bella thought how different from her own sunny little
      wedding, and wept. Mrs Milvey overflowed with pity, and wept too. The
      dolls’ dressmaker, with her hands before her face, wept in her golden
      bower. Reading in a low clear voice, and bending over Eugene, who kept his
      eyes upon him, Mr Milvey did his office with suitable simplicity. As the
      bridegroom could not move his hand, they touched his fingers with the
      ring, and so put it on the bride. When the two plighted their troth, she
      laid her hand on his and kept it there. When the ceremony was done, and
      all the rest departed from the room, she drew her arm under his head, and
      laid her own head down upon the pillow by his side.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c64:p101.text:
‘Now, scoundrel,’ he pursued, ‘I am going to finish. You supposed me just
      now, to be the possessor of my father’s property.—So I am. But
      through any act of my father’s, or by any right I have? No. Through the
      munificence of Mr Boffin. The conditions that he made with me, before
      parting with the secret of the Dutch bottle, were, that I should take the
      fortune, and that he should take his Mound and no more. I owe everything I
      possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness,
      goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin. And
      when, knowing what I knew, I saw such a mud-worm as you presume to rise in
      this house against this noble soul, the wonder is,’ added John Harmon
      through his clenched teeth, and with a very ugly turn indeed on Wegg’s
      cravat, ‘that I didn’t try to twist your head off, and fling  that  out of
      window! So. That’s the last short speech, do you understand?’

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?
c17:p5.summary: The Secretary catalogs individual beggars seeking Boffin's charity—daughters of officers, distressed wives and husbands, those claiming divine inspiration, independent beggars offering loans, and those threatening suicide—each category satirically anatomized.
c17:p5.best_quote: they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf

c27:p51.text:
The consideration of Mrs Boffin had clothed Mr Sloppy in a suit of black,
      on which the tailor had received personal directions from Rokesmith to
      expend the utmost cunning of his art, with a view to the concealment of
      the cohering and sustaining buttons. But, so much more powerful were the
      frailties of Sloppy’s form than the strongest resources of tailoring
      science, that he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way
      of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a
      hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators. The
      artistic taste of some unknown hatter had furnished him with a hatband of
      wholesale capacity which was fluted behind, from the crown of his hat to
      the brim, and terminated in a black bunch, from which the imagination
      shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted. Some special powers with which
      his legs were endowed, had already hitched up his glossy trousers at the
      ankles, and bagged them at the knees; while similar gifts in his arms had
      raised his coat-sleeves from his wrists and accumulated them at his
      elbows. Thus set forth, with the additional embellishments of a very
      little tail to his coat, and a yawning gulf at his waistband, Sloppy stood
      confessed.

c20:p51.text:
‘My love,’ says Lady Tippins, ‘compose yourself; we’ll bring him in.’ And
      Lady Tippins really does work, and work the Veneering horses too; for she
      clatters about town all day, calling upon everybody she knows, and showing
      her entertaining powers and green fan to immense advantage, by rattling on
      with, My dear soul, what do you think? What do you suppose me to be?
      You’ll never guess. I’m pretending to be an electioneering agent. And for
      what place of all places? Pocket-Breaches. And why? Because the dearest
      friend I have in the world has bought it. And who is the dearest friend I
      have in the world? A man of the name of Veneering. Not omitting his wife,
      who is the other dearest friend I have in the world; and I positively
      declare I forgot their baby, who is the other. And we are carrying on this
      little farce to keep up appearances, and isn’t it refreshing! Then, my
      precious child, the fun of it is that nobody knows who these Veneerings
      are, and that they know nobody, and that they have a house out of the
      Tales of the Genii, and give dinners out of the Arabian Nights. Curious to
      see ’em, my dear? Say you’ll know ’em. Come and dine with ’em. They shan’t
      bore you. Say who shall meet you. We’ll make up a party of our own, and
      I’ll engage that they shall not interfere with you for one single moment.
      You really ought to see their gold and silver camels. I call their
      dinner-table, the Caravan. Do come and dine with my Veneerings, my own
      Veneerings, my exclusive property, the dearest friends I have in the
      world! And above all, my dear, be sure you promise me your vote and
      interest and all sorts of plumpers for Pocket-Breaches; for we couldn’t
      think of spending sixpence on it, my love, and can only consent to be
      brought in by the spontaneous thingummies of the incorruptible
      whatdoyoucallums.

c44:p10.text:
The haggard head floated up the dark staircase, and softly descended
      nearer to the floor outside the outer door of the chambers. The doors of
      the rooms within, appeared to be standing open. There were rays of
      candlelight from one of them, and there was the sound of a footstep going
      about. There were two voices. The words they uttered were not
      distinguishable, but they were both the voices of men. In a few moments
      the voices were silent, and there was no sound of footstep, and the inner

      awake, staring and listening in the darkness outside the door as he spoke
      of it, he might have been less disposed to sleep, through the remainder of
      the night.
